content: People with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) require insulin therapy to survive. However, it remains unclear whether any specific type of ultra-long-acting or long-acting insulin analogues offers advantages, particularly in reducing the risk of diabetes-related complications or hypoglycemia. The objective of this study was to compare the long-term effects of ultra-long-acting or long-acting insulin analogues with NPH insulin (neutral protamine Hagedorn) or other ultra-long-acting or long-acting insulin analogues in individuals with T1DM. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. They also reviewed reference lists of systematic reviews, articles, and health technology assessment reports. Additional data were sought from pharmaceutical companies, regulatory agencies such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and clinical study reports (CSRs). The last search was conducted on August 24, 2020. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) lasting 24 weeks or longer that compared one ultra-long-acting or long-acting insulin analogue with NPH insulin or another ultra-long-acting or long-acting insulin analogue in people with T1DM. Two reviewers assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane 'Risk of Bias' 2 (RoB 2) tool and extracted data. The primary outcomes included all-cause mortality, health-related quality of life (QoL), severe hypoglycemia, non-fatal myocardial infarction (NFMI) or stroke (NFS), severe nocturnal hypoglycemia, serious adverse events (SAEs), and glycosylated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c). Meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model, and results were expressed as risk ratios (RRs), odds ratios (ORs), or mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and prediction intervals. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 26 RCTs were included, involving 8,784 participants. Among these, 2,428 participants received NPH insulin, 2,889 received insulin detemir, 2,095 received insulin glargine, and 1,372 received insulin degludec. Eight studies (21% of participants) included children. The duration of interventions ranged from 24 to 104 weeks. Insulin degludec versus NPH insulin: No studies directly compared insulin degludec with NPH insulin. Insulin detemir versus NPH insulin (9 RCTs): Five deaths were reported in the insulin detemir group in two studies involving adults (Peto OR 4.97, 95% CI 0.79 to 31.38; moderate-certainty evidence). Three studies (870 participants) reported no significant differences in QoL between the two groups (low-certainty evidence). Severe hypoglycemia was less frequent in the insulin detemir group (8.5%) compared to the NPH insulin group (11.5%) (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.92; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the 95% prediction interval (0.34 to 1.39) suggested inconsistency. One participant in the insulin detemir group experienced a non-fatal myocardial infarction (NFMI), while none in the NPH insulin group did (low-certainty evidence). No studies reported non-fatal strokes (NFS). Serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 7.9% of participants in the insulin detemir group and 8.2% in the NPH insulin group (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.21; moderate-certainty evidence). Severe nocturnal hypoglycemia was observed in 3.8% of participants in the insulin detemir group compared to 5.4% in the NPH insulin group (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.17; moderate-certainty evidence). The mean difference in HbA1c between the two groups was 0.01% (95% CI -0.1 to 0.1; moderate-certainty evidence). Insulin glargine versus NPH insulin (9 RCTs): One death occurred in the NPH insulin group (Peto OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.00 to 6.98; moderate-certainty evidence). Four studies (1,013 participants) reported no significant differences in QoL between the two groups (low-certainty evidence). Severe hypoglycemia occurred in 10.2% of participants in the insulin glargine group compared to 12.5% in the NPH insulin group (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.04; moderate-certainty evidence). No participants experienced NFMI, and one participant in the NPH insulin group experienced a non-fatal stroke (low-certainty evidence). SAEs occurred in 9.6% of participants in the insulin glargine group and 10.0% in the NPH insulin group (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.84; moderate-certainty evidence). Severe nocturnal hypoglycemia was observed in 7.4% of participants in the insulin glargine group compared to 8.7% in the NPH insulin group (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.12; moderate-certainty evidence). The mean difference in HbA1c between the two groups was 0.02% (95% CI -0.1 to 0.1; moderate-certainty evidence). Comparisons between ultra-long-acting insulin analogues: Insulin detemir versus insulin glargine (2 RCTs), insulin degludec versus insulin detemir (2 RCTs), and insulin degludec versus insulin glargine (4 RCTs) showed no clinically relevant differences in any primary outcomes. No significant differences were observed between children and adults in any of the comparisons. Conclusions: Insulin detemir was associated with a lower risk of severe hypoglycemia compared to NPH insulin (moderate-certainty evidence), but the prediction interval suggested inconsistency. Neither insulin detemir nor insulin glargine showed significant benefits or harms for severe nocturnal hypoglycemia compared to NPH insulin. For other primary outcomes, including QoL, macrovascular and microvascular complications, and HbA1c, no clinically meaningful differences were observed. Data on patient-important outcomes were limited, and no significant differences were found between children and adults.
